content.title: About
content.content: Beef and vegetables, Hawaiian style is a dish that combines tender strips of beef, fresh vegetables (bell pepper, carrot, pineapple) and a fragrant sauce made from soy sauce, ginger and coconut milk. It cooks quickly, retains bright flavors and evokes the tropical culinary vibe of Hawaii.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Hawaiian cooking often uses pineapple, which adds a sweet note and helps tenderize meat.
Beef marinated in soy sauce and ginger absorbs flavors faster, a technique common in poke dishes.
The dish is frequently served over rice or noodles, but the original Hawaiian version is eaten with leafy greens.
The sweet‑salty balance (pineapple and soy sauce) reflects the harmony of flavors typical of Hawaiian cuisine.
Hawaiian chefs usually use vegetables harvested the same day to keep a crisp texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Bell pepper and carrot are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Benefits of coconut milk
items.content: Coconut milk contains medium‑chain triglycerides that can provide a quick energy source.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts of beef can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut milk.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce adds a significant amount of salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogenic bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically over steamed rice, noodles, or a bed of lettuce. Garnish with fresh pineapple, cilantro and a squeeze of lime for extra brightness. Leftovers store in the fridge and reheat in a skillet or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Toasted multigrain bread is a whole‑grain loaf made from a blend of different cereals (wheat, rye, oats, barley, sunflower seeds, etc.) and lightly toasted to a golden crust. It has a rich nutty aroma, a crunchy crust and a dense yet tender crumb. This bread is commonly used as a base for sandwiches, snacks and soup accompaniments.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Multigrain bread contains more fiber and micronutrients than standard white bread.
Toasting enhances flavor through the Maillard reaction, creating new taste compounds.
The mix often includes flax and pumpkin seeds, which are high in omega‑3 fatty acids.
Such breads have a long tradition in European countries that value grain diversity.
A toasted crust stays crisp longer when the loaf is stored in a dry environment.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide steady energy and maintain stable glucose levels.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Seeds added to the dough supply omega‑3 and omega‑6 fatty acids beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Multigrain bread provides B1, B2, B3 and folate, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies magnesium, iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for bones, muscles and immunity.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to wheat, rye or other grains used in the loaf.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The bread contains gluten, so it should be avoided by people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Toasted breads are often salted; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite its benefits, the bread is calorie‑dense; portions should be moderate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted multigrain bread works great for sandwiches with avocado, cream cheese, turkey or vegetables. It can be used for croutons, crumbled into salads, or served alongside soups. For a softer bite, lightly brush the slices with olive oil before toasting.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, place it in an airtight container and refrigerate, where it stays fresh for up to a week. Freeze individual slices if you need to keep it for a longer period.

content.title: About
content.content: Oat bunches are whole oat grains that have been steamed and rolled into flakes. They retain most of the fiber, vitamins, and minerals of whole oat groats and have a mild, slightly nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 10,000 years.
Oat flakes are a common base for muesli and granola mixes.
Oats belong to the grass family and are related to wheat and barley, but contain more beta‑glucans.
Modern processing often keeps the bran, making most oat flakes whole‑grain.
Oats thrive in temperate climates and require moderate moisture.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans are soluble fibers that help lower cholesterol and support heart health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Oat flakes release glucose slowly, providing sustained energy and prolonged satiety.

items.title: Contains vitamin B1 and magnesium
items.content: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) aids energy metabolism, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with refined grains, oat flakes have a lower GI, which is beneficial for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Pure oats are gluten‑free, but they are often processed alongside wheat; choose certified gluten‑free oats if you have celiac disease.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Oats contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in very large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook oat flakes with milk, water, or plant‑based milk, add them to smoothies, yogurt, baked goods, or use as a coating. Soaking for 10‑30 minutes yields a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store flakes in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

corn-canned-reduced-sodium-cooked-no-add.title: Corn, canned, reduced sodium, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sodium canned corn is a ready‑to‑eat product made from mature corn kernels that are cooked, lightly salted, and sealed in airtight cans. No fat is added during processing, making it a convenient low‑salt option for quick meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn has been cultivated for more than 7,000 years and is one of the world’s oldest staple crops.
Canning preserves most B‑vitamins and antioxidants such as lutein.
Reduced‑sodium versions are ideal for people watching their salt intake.
Corn provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.
In the United States canned corn is a common ingredient in salads, chowders, and chili.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes regular bowel movements, helps maintain satiety, and supports stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect eye health and reduce oxidative stress in cells.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt content is beneficial for blood‑pressure control and cardiovascular risk reduction.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate (B9) aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Provides magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle function and help maintain electrolyte balance.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rash to respiratory symptoms.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Although unsweetened, the natural sugars in corn can affect blood glucose levels in people with diabetes; portion control is advised.

items.title: Can integrity
items.content: If the can is damaged or the product is stored for too long after opening, oxidation may occur; consume within the recommended time.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the corn straight from the can, add it to salads, soups, stews, omelets, or use it as a filling for tacos and burritos. It can also be quickly warmed in a skillet with herbs and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer leftovers to an airtight container and refrigerate for 3–4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Doughnut NFS (2824) is a classic fried sweet pastry shaped as a ring and finished with glaze or sprinkles. It is made from wheat flour, sugar, eggs, milk and yeast, then deep‑fried until golden and coated with sugar glaze, chocolate or various toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts appeared in Europe in the 17th century and quickly became popular street food.
In the United States they are called "donuts" and can be ring‑shaped or filled with jam, custard, or cream.
There are over 100 glaze and topping variations, from classic sugar to bright candy crumbs.
In Japan, doughnuts often contain a sweet red‑bean paste (anko) filling.
Doughnuts are commonly paired with coffee as a traditional breakfast.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The carbohydrates in doughnuts are rapidly digested, providing an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Contains some protein
items.content: Eggs and milk in the recipe contribute a modest amount of animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast and whole‑grain flour (when used) can supply B1, B2 and niacin.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Deep‑frying adds trans‑fatty acids and saturated fats, which are unfavorable for heart health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, making doughnuts unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A single medium doughnut can contain 250–350 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doughnuts are usually enjoyed as a dessert or snack, often with coffee or tea. They can be split and filled with cream, jam, or custard. For a lighter option, choose unglazed or lightly topped versions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store doughnuts in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag and reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, fried, with beef is a popular Asian dish consisting of cooked rice stir‑fried with pieces of beef, vegetables and soy sauce. It offers a savory meat flavor, aromatic spices and a subtle sweetness from the sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is commonly served at street stalls and fast‑food restaurants throughout Southeast Asia.
Traditional recipes include onion, carrot, peas and egg, but variations may add pineapple, corn or mushrooms.
High‑heat wok cooking preserves a slightly crunchy texture of the rice grains.
In Japan a similar dish is called “chahan” (チャーハン).
The recipe scales easily from a home‑cooked portion to large cafeteria batches.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Beef provides a complete set of amino acids that support muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Rice delivers complex carbohydrates that release energy gradually.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and soy sauce are rich in B12, niacin and riboflavin, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc and phosphorus, which support immunity and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables such as carrots and peas add beta‑carotene and vitamin C.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can significantly increase salt intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Stir‑frying with a lot of oil can make the dish calorie‑dense and high in saturated fats.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to soy sauce.

items.title: Undercooked meat risk
items.content: Insufficiently cooked beef may harbor pathogenic bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, usually in individual bowls. It pairs well with fresh vegetable salads, pickled ginger or a spicy chili sauce. To reduce sodium, choose low‑salt soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a hot pan to restore the rice’s slight crispness.
